result: The authors developed and optimized a 3D automated surface mapping system for mechanical characterization of mouse femoral condyle cartilage with high spatial resolution, performing repeated indentation mappings at 31 predefined positions distributed over the medial and lateral femoral condyles.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C44, C45, C51-C53, C164-C165 collectively describe the development and optimization of the automated indentation mapping system. The methodology is clearly described with specific parameters (31 positions, 20 μm depth, 0.3 mm spherical indenter), and the system was designed to assess load-bearing regions of femoral condyles. The experimental design is well-documented and reproducible.

result: The automated indentation mapping technique demonstrated high reproducibility with only 2.26% error rate, 4.7% coefficient of variation, and ICC values ranging from 0.971-0.974, with typical stress-relaxation behavior observed and consistency among repeated measurements.
evaluation: Claims C6, C54-C60, C111-C112 provide strong quantitative evidence for the reproducibility of the technique. The low error rate (2.26%), low coefficient of variation (4.7%), and high ICC values (>0.97) with tight confidence intervals demonstrate excellent test-retest reliability. The data is supported by Figure 1B showing consistent force-relaxation curves across repeated measures.

result: Site-specific variations in peak force were identified across femoral condyle locations, with the medial condyle yielding approximately two times higher peak forces than the lateral condyle, and both condyles showing decreased forces posteriorly.
evaluation: Claims C61-C68, C113-C115 are well-supported by quantitative data showing significant spatial heterogeneity in peak forces. The medial condyle showed forces ranging from 0.15-0.294 N versus 0.07-0.15 N for lateral condyle (p<0.0001). The 20% decrease in Med/Post versus Med/Ant (p<0.01) is statistically significant. Data is visualized in Figure 1D and Table 2.

result: Needle probing (NP) cartilage thickness measurements were validated against high-resolution 3D XRM imaging, showing highly significant correlation (R=0.842, p<0.0001) with only 6.8 μm average difference and 2.58% failure rate.
evaluation: Claims C5, C7, C46, C71-C79, C123-C124 demonstrate strong validation of the NP technique. The high correlation (R=0.842, n=302, p<0.0001), small systematic bias (6.8 μm = 1.55 voxels), and low failure rate (2.58%) provide robust evidence. The Bland-Altman analysis (Figure 2E) and site-specific comparisons (Figure 2F) support the agreement between methods. The 3D visualization confirmed needle probe reached subchondral bone.

result: Spatial heterogeneities in cartilage thickness were identified, with the lateral condyle showing significant variation (46-76 μm, p<0.0001) while the medial condyle was more uniform (36-45 μm, p=0.06), and the medial condyle was significantly thinner than the lateral condyle in both anterior and posterior sub-regions.
evaluation: Claims C80-C83, C128-C129 are supported by quantitative thickness measurements from both NP and XRM (Tables 3-4). The significant spatial heterogeneity in lateral condyle (p<0.0001) versus uniform medial condyle (p=0.06) is statistically demonstrated. The medial-lateral difference is consistent with prior literature (C128-C129) and shown in both anteroposterior sub-regions (p<0.0001).

result: Pairwise analysis revealed significant negative correlation between peak force and thickness (lateral R=-0.554, medial R=-0.463, both p<0.001), but when accounting for thickness using Hayes elastic model at 20% strain, instantaneous modulus showed no correlation with thickness and differed significantly between condyles (p<0.001) but not within condyle sub-regions.
evaluation: Claims C87-C93, C120 demonstrate the importance of accounting for thickness in mechanical measurements. The negative correlations between peak force and thickness are statistically significant and visualized in Figure 3A-B. After applying Hayes model corrections, the instantaneous modulus becomes independent of thickness (Figure 3C-D), validating the analytical approach. The between-condyle differences (p<0.001) without within-condyle differences support the conclusion that thickness is a contributing but not sole factor.

result: The technique successfully identified regional biomechanical changes in Prg4−/− mice compared to controls, with increased cartilage thickness on both condyles (lateral: 67.9±3.5 μm, p=0.032; medial: 56.3±3.7 μm, p<0.001) and significantly decreased stiffness confined to the medial condyle (8.67±1.79 MPa vs 19.52±2.44 MPa, p<0.001), with no significant differences in lateral condyle stiffness.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C48-C49, C94, C101-C104, C106-C108, C134, C142, C157 are well-supported by quantitative comparisons between genotypes. The thickness increases are statistically significant with appropriate p-values. The medial-specific reduction in stiffness (55% decrease, p<0.001) versus non-significant lateral changes (p=0.187) demonstrates regional sensitivity of the technique. Heat maps in Figure 4A-B show reproducibility across specimens. The Hayes model fit well (RMSE: 0.017±0.007 MPa for controls, 0.010±0.003 MPa for Prg4−/−).

result: XRM analysis of contralateral femoral condyles not subjected to biomechanical testing yielded mean thicknesses of 40.63±3.14 μm (medial) and 56.99±6.26 μm (lateral), suggesting repeated indentations did not compromise cartilage but NP may have caused tissue swelling affecting subsequent XRM measurements.
evaluation: Claims C84-C86 provide important validation data. The contralateral measurements are comparable to site-specific NP values but slightly lower than post-NP XRM values, supporting the inference that indentation did not damage tissue but NP may have caused swelling. This is a reasonable interpretation given the 6.8 μm systematic difference between NP and XRM (C77) and the physical evidence of NP deformities visible in XRM images (Figure 2A).

result: The Hayes elastic model fit mouse cartilage data with high accuracy (RMSE: 0.017±0.007 MPa for controls, 0.010±0.003 MPa for Prg4−/−), though apparent modulus values were about an order of magnitude larger than previous AFM studies, attributed to differences in compression rate (1 μm/s vs 20 μm/s) and indentation scale (micro- vs nano-indentation).
evaluation: Claims C105, C136-C141 demonstrate good model fit with low RMSE values. The comparison to Coles et al. 2010 is appropriate, and the explanation for the order-of-magnitude difference (compression rate, indentation scale, anatomical location) is scientifically sound and supported by citation to Bae et al. 2006. The thickness values are consistent with Karamchedu et al. 2016, providing additional validation.

result: The optimized sample mounting and needle probing protocols enabled unprecedented quantitative mapping of mechanical behavior and cartilage thickness on load-bearing regions of mouse distal femurs with higher spatial density compared to previous studies.
evaluation: Claims C109-C110, C155-C156 are supported by the comprehensive methodology and results. The 31-position mapping grid with site-specific thickness measurements represents an advance over previous studies (Woods et al. 2021, Lavoie et al. 2015) that used non-load-bearing regions or mean thickness values. The load-bearing region assessment is anatomically justified by mouse knee kinematics (C35-C37).

result: The medial-specific reduction in instantaneous modulus in Prg4−/− mice is attributed to greater thickening (41% vs 12.6% in lateral) and compromised structural integrity having larger functional impact on the main load-bearing medial compartment, with disrupted collagen fibril organization likely affecting fluid pressurization under rapid loading.
evaluation: Claims C143-C150 provide a mechanistic interpretation supported by the data and literature. The differential thickening (41% medial vs 12.6% lateral) is quantified from the results. The explanation involving disrupted collagen organization (Jay et al. 2007), fluid pressurization, and load-bearing function is scientifically sound and consistent with cartilage biomechanics principles (Armstrong 1986, Julkunen et al. 2008, Korhonen et al. 2002). However, this remains an inference as collagen organization was not directly measured in this study.

result: The study addresses the often-overlooked effect of site-specific cartilage geometry on indentation measurements, demonstrating that thickness variations affect peak forces at fixed indentation depth, with thinner cartilage yielding higher forces, and that knowledge of thickness variations improves reliability of indentation assessment despite potential substrate effects.
evaluation: Claims C69-C70, C118-C119, C121-C122, C125-C126, C130-C132 are well-supported by the data and literature. The negative correlation between thickness and peak force (C87) validates the concern. The authors appropriately acknowledge the substrate effect limitation (Julkunen et al. 2008) while arguing that site-specific thickness knowledge improves interpretation. The resolution differences between Mach-1 (0.5 μm) and XRM (4.39 μm) and partial volume artifacts are reasonable explanations for measurement variations.

result: The technique comprehensively characterized cartilage function in mouse femoral condyles and has potential to improve understanding of tissue structure-function interplay in mouse models of repair and disease, with microscale indentation providing more comprehensive characterization of mechanical properties.
evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C50, C158-C159 represent reasonable conclusions based on the demonstrated capabilities of the technique. The comprehensive characterization is evidenced by the spatial mapping of both thickness and mechanical properties. However, the 'potential' language appropriately indicates these are forward-looking statements. The technique's utility was demonstrated in the Prg4−/− model, supporting the claim it could be applied to other models.

result: Study limitations include evaluation of only distal femoral condyles (not proximal tibia), single timepoint analysis, and use of elastic model rather than more complex biphasic/poroviscoelastic models that could capture time-dependent behavior.
evaluation: Claims C151-C154 appropriately acknowledge study limitations. The single timepoint limitation is valid given that aging and degeneration affect cartilage properties (supported by citations). The recommendation for more complex models (Mow et al. 1980, Julkunen et al. 2009b) is reasonable given cartilage's biphasic nature, though the Hayes model performed well for the instantaneous response measured here.

result: There was no significant variation in mean thickness of healthy cartilage over a condyle surface, justifying comparison of biomechanical parameters between matched regions when assessing degeneration.
evaluation: Claim C133 appears to contradict earlier findings. C80 states lateral condyle showed significant spatial heterogeneity (p<0.0001, range 46-76 μm), while C133 claims no significant variation. The statement may refer to anteroposterior sub-regions (C82: no significant differences within condyles when comparing anterior vs posterior), but the wording is ambiguous. This needs clarification as it affects the validity of the regional comparison approach.
